qs.q: Which blood group system is most frequently associated with delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions that present with a rapid drop in hemoglobin but negative initial antibody screens?
qs.e: The Kidd system is the classic cause of delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions. Antibodies fade quickly, screen negative, then surge after re-exposure causing rapid intravascular hemolysis.
qs.s: Expert Immunohematology Assessment — Study Notes: MCQs

qs.q: The presence or absence of which specific antigen primarily defines the Rhesus (Rh) blood group system?
qs.e: The Rh system is based primarily on the presence or absence of the D antigen. The Kell antigen belongs to an entirely separate blood group system.
qs.s: Blood Grouping and Blood Typing — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: During blood group testing, a patient's blood sample shows agglutination when mixed with both anti-A and anti-B antibodies. What is the blood type?
qs.e: Agglutination with both anti-A and anti-B antibodies indicates that the blood type is AB. Type O shows no agglutination with either reagent.
qs.s: Blood Grouping and Blood Typing — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Who discovered the ABO human blood groups in 1901, proving that blood clumping is an immunological reaction?
qs.e: Prof. Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO human blood groups in 1901 and found that blood clumping was an immunological reaction. This discovery made it possible to determine blood types, earning him a Nobel prize.

qs.q: Which immunoglobulin class typically comprises naturally occurring antibodies found in individuals lacking the corresponding ABO blood group antigen?
qs.e: Naturally occurring antibodies in the ABO system are typically IgM, which are present in the plasma even without prior transfusion exposure. In contrast, Rh system antibodies are usually IgG and result from immune stimulation.
qs.s: Transfusion: Governance, Donor Selection & Blood Groups — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which blood group system causes the most severe and potentially fatal transfusion reactions due to naturally occurring antibodies?
qs.e: ABO incompatibility causes the most severe and potentially fatal transfusion reactions because its antibodies are naturally occurring. Other systems like Rh require prior sensitisation to mount significant immune responses.
qs.s: Blood Transfusion: ABO, Rh Blood Groups, Compatibility & HDN — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: What is the universal plasma donor blood group?
qs.e: AB positive is the universal plasma donor because its plasma contains no anti-A or anti-B antibodies. Conversely, O negative is the universal red blood cell donor.
qs.s: Blood Transfusion: ABO, Rh Blood Groups, Compatibility & HDN — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which blood group system is notable for having Duffy-null individuals who are resistant to Plasmodium vivax malaria?
qs.e: Duffy-null individuals possess resistance to Plasmodium vivax malaria, placing the Duffy system fourth in clinical significance. The Kell system ranks third and is a strong immunogen.
qs.s: Blood Transfusion: ABO, Rh Blood Groups, Compatibility & HDN — Notes: MCQs

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Blood groups are surface antigens on red cells that determine compatibility for transfusion and pregnancy. They arise from carbohydrate or protein differences encoded by ABO and Rh genes. Clinicians use group knowledge to prevent hemolysis and manage immune-mediated disease.

sections.p: The ABO system classifies red cells as A, B, AB or O based on the presence of A and B antigens; the Rh system adds D antigen positivity or negativity.
b: Naturally occurring anti‑A or anti‑B IgM antibodies develop early in life

sections.p: A and B antigens are carbohydrate chains added to the H antigen by specific glycosyltransferases. Rh D is a membrane protein that transports ions.
b: ABO genes on chromosome 9, Rh genes on chromosome 1
Antibodies are IgM and do not cross the placenta

sections.p: Expression of ABO enzymes is tissue‑specific; Rh D expression is regulated during erythropoiesis. No hormonal control is needed for antigen presence.
b: No known acute up‑ or down‑regulation

sections.p: Incompatible transfusion or pregnancy can trigger immune hemolysis. Auto‑ or allo‑antibodies may form after sensitisation (transfusion, pregnancy, transplantation).
b: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction: fever, flank pain, dark urine
Hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN): maternal anti‑D IgG crosses placenta

sections.p: Correct matching prevents life‑threatening hemolysis. Certain groups influence disease risk (e.g., severe malaria in O, thrombosis in non‑O).
b: Rh‑negative mother with Rh‑positive fetus → HDN
Group O higher risk of peptic ulcer disease

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden dark urine, back pain, or hypotension after transfusion; newborn jaundice with anemia; unexplained hemolysis

faq.q: Why can O‑negative blood be given to anyone in an emergency?
faq.a: It lacks A, B, and D antigens, so no pre‑formed antibodies in the recipient will react.

faq.q: What causes hemolytic disease of the newborn?
faq.a: Maternal IgG anti‑D (or anti‑A/B) crosses the placenta and destroys fetal red cells.

faq.q: Can a person change their blood group?
faq.a: No, ABO and Rh are genetically fixed; only acquired antibodies can change serology.
